figures.caption: Figure 1: 4-bit encodings. (a) The 15 E2M1 values are dense near zero and sparse near the maximum, unlike the uniform grid of symmetric INT4 (rescaled here to the same maximum, 6). (b) MXFP4 shares one power-of-two (E8M0) scale among 32 elements. NVFP4 uses one FP8 (E4M3) scale per 16 elements plus an FP32 tensor scale, so it spends 0.25 bit more per element on scales. Cell widths are proportional to bits.

Figure 2: Input data. (a) Expert hypnogram of one Sleep-EDF night (SC4001), restricted to the scored window (30 minutes of wake before the first and after the last sleep epoch). N3 is drawn in dark blue and REM in red. (b) One representative 30-second Fpz–Cz epoch per stage (100 Hz), drawn on a common ±120 µV axis. The models receive the raw epoch. W4A4 formats quantize it to 4 bits in the first layer.

Table 1: Evaluated formats. Scales are given for weights and for activations. Bits/w: bits per weight, including block or channel scales (K: reduction length of the layer); the single FP32 tensor scale of NVFP4 is not counted. The INT4-g32 emulation keeps FP32 group scales. A: activations. †Non-standard block size, used as an ablation.

Table 3: Post-training quantization on Sleep-EDF-78 (Fpz–Cz, 10-fold subject-wise CV, 3 training seeds). MF1: pooled Macro-F1 (%), mean over seeds. ∆MF1: per-subject paired difference to FP32 in percentage points (pp), averaged over seeds, mean and bootstrap 95% CI over n = 78 subjects; ∗/∗∗: Holm-corrected Wilcoxon signed-rank p < 0.05/0.01 (family of 20 conditions per model). Flip: % of 30-s epochs whose predicted stage differs from FP32 (pooled over test epochs per seed, mean over seeds). KiB: packed weights including scale metadata and FP32 biases. W/A: weight/activation bits. †Non-standard block size (ablation). All formats are emulated: values are rounded exactly to each format, and the arithmetic is FP32 (native FP16/BF16 is checked in Section 3.7).

Figure 4: Change in Macro-F1 relative to FP32 for every condition on Sleep-EDF-78: mean and 95% bootstrap CI over the 78 test subjects of the per-subject paired change, averaged over three seeds. Filled markers: Holm-corrected Wilcoxon p < 0.05 (20 conditions per model). Open markers: not significant. Label colors mark format families. Rows are grouped into 16- and 8-bit formats plus weight-only INT4 (top), block-scaled 4-bit formats (middle), and recovery strategies with the QAT control (bottom). W only: weights quantized, activations in FP32 (BF16 for INT4-g32). (a) SleepCNN loses 1.98–3.04 pp under every W4A4 format. (b) ContextSleepNet loses at most 1.19 pp, and no condition is significant after correction.

Figure 5: Same-encoder ablation. ∆MF1 of each model relative to its own FP32 model (mean and 95% bootstrap CI over subjects; per-subject paired, three seeds). EncoderNet is ContextSleepNet without its temporal layers. FP8 f/l: FP8 first and last layers. The legend in (a) applies to both panels. (a) Sleep-EDF-78 (n = 78): EncoderNet loses much less than SleepCNN and only slightly more than ContextSleepNet. (b) Sleep-EDF-20 (n = 20): under MXFP4, the two models with the larger encoder lose more than SleepCNN. With NVFP4-16 and FP8 first/last layers, all three models stay close to FP32.

Figure 6: Where the 4-bit error arises. (a) ∆MF1 when a single layer is quantized to W4A4 and all others stay in FP32 (mean and 95% CI). For SleepCNN, most of the loss comes from conv1, the layer that quantizes the raw EEG. (b, c) Change of the row-normalized confusion matrix from FP32 to MXFP4-32 W4A4 (pooled test epochs, mean over seeds). Entries are percentage points of each true stage, so each row sums to zero up to rounding. Both models move true N3 epochs into N2. SleepCNN also moves N2 and REM epochs into N1.

Figure 7: Recovering W4A4 accuracy on Sleep-EDF-78 (∆MF1 vs FP32; mean and 95% CI). Bar color gives the format (red: MXFP4-32; purple: NVFP4-16). Lighter shades: FP8 first layer, and FP8 first and last layers; both need no retraining. Hatched: FT→PTQ, the FP32+FT model quantized with the same PTQ. Blue: QAT. Gray band and dashed line: 95% CI and mean of the matched control (FP32+FT, fine-tuned for the same five training epochs as QAT). QAT should be judged against this control and against FT→PTQ, not against FP32.

Table 4: Recovering W4A4 accuracy. FP8 first/last: first (raw-EEG input) and last layer in FP8-E4M3 W8A8, all other layers 4-bit. QAT: quantization-aware fine-tuning for five training epochs with the straight-through estimator. FP32+FT: the same fine-tuning without quantization (matched control). FT→PTQ: the FP32+FT model followed by the same PTQ. ∆MF1 vs FP32 as in Table 3. “vs FP32+FT”: QAT (or FT→PTQ) minus the control, per-subject paired. Stars mark Holm-corrected Wilcoxon p < 0.05/0.01: in the ∆MF1 column within the 20-condition family of each model, and in the “vs FP32+FT” column within the two QAT comparisons of each model. FT→PTQ rows lie outside both families and carry no stars. GBOPs: ∑ℓMACsℓ bwba per 30-s epoch, in 109.

Table 5: Subject-level view: distribution of per-(subject, seed) ∆MF1 (pp; n = 234) and epoch flip rate (defined as in Table 3). Retraining noise: FP32 versus FP32 trained with another seed on the same folds, both orders of each of the three seed pairs (n = 468, symmetric around zero); it is the reference for both the tail and the flip rate. P5: 5th percentile; <−5: share of subject–seed pairs losing more than 5 pp.

Figure 8: Subject-level view. (a, b) Distribution of ∆MF1 per (subject, seed) pair (n = 234) for selected conditions and for retraining noise (FP32 versus FP32 trained with another seed; both orders of each seed pair, n = 468). Boxes: interquartile range and median; whiskers: 5th–95th percentiles; dots: values beyond the whiskers. FP8 f/l: FP8 first and last layers. (c) Per-subject ∆MF1 under 4-bit PTQ (seed-averaged) of SleepCNN against ContextSleepNet. ρ: Spearman correlation; dashed line: identity. The same subjects lose accuracy in both architectures. (d) The same plot for retraining noise (three seed pairs, one marker shape each): the signed changes of the two architectures do not agree. Their sign is arbitrary, so this panel does not rule out that the same subjects are unstable in both models (Section 4.6).
Table 7: Sleep stages: main EEG criteria (simplified from [1, 2]) and share of the 195,469 epochs used here.

Figure 9: Signal background. (a) Electrode positions of the international 10–20 system (top view, nose up). Along the midline, Fpz lies 10% of the nasion–inion distance from the nasion, and neighboring electrodes are 20% apart. The model input is the Fpz–Cz derivation (red). The second Sleep-EDF EEG derivation, Pz–Oz (dashed), is not used. (b) Mean log power spectral density of the Fpz–Cz signal per stage over all 195,469 epochs, in dB relative to 1 µV2/Hz before normalization (Welch’s method, 2.56-s Hann windows, 50% overlap; notebook Cell 21). Shaded: delta, theta, alpha, sigma, and beta bands. The band edges are approximate, because the sigma band overlaps the conventional alpha and beta ranges.

Figure 10: The three architectures. In (a) and (b), box width grows with the number of channels and box height with the sequence length (both compressed). Vectors are drawn as thin boxes. (a) SleepCNN classifies each 30-s epoch on its own. (b) EncoderNet, the ablation model (Section 3.7), applies the per-epoch encoder of ContextSleepNet (dashed frame) and a linear classifier to each epoch. It uses no information from neighboring epochs. (c) ContextSleepNet runs the same encoder on every epoch of the night. It combines the 128-dimensional embeddings with four residual dilated temporal convolutions. (d) With kernel 3 and dilations 1, 2, 4, and 8, the label of epoch t depends on epochs t −15 to t +15. Block labels: k, kernel size; s, stride (both in samples at 100 Hz; stride 1 if omitted); d, dilation of the temporal convolutions in epochs. Numbers under the blocks are output shapes (channels × length; L: number of epochs). The first layer (red), which receives the raw EEG, is the most sensitive to 4-bit quantization (Section 4.4). The red labels give its share of all MACs in SleepCNN and in EncoderNet (29.2% in ContextSleepNet). Block diagrams use the PlotNeuralNet TikZ styles [49].

Table 8: Results on the nested Sleep-EDF-20 subset (subjects 0–19; 42,307 epochs), retrained with the same pipeline, three seeds, and 10-fold subject-wise CV (two test subjects per fold). ∆MF1 vs the FP32 model of the same architecture (pp, mean and 95% bootstrap CI over n = 20 subjects). ∗/∗∗: Holm-corrected Wilcoxon p < 0.05/0.01 within each model (17 conditions). Sleep-EDF-20 is a subset of Sleep-EDF-78, so this is not an independent replication.

Table 9: Same-encoder ablation on Sleep-EDF-78. EncoderNet is ContextSleepNet without the temporal convolutions (same encoder, classifier, training and calibration). ∆MF1 of each model relative to its own FP32 model (per-subject paired, mean over 3 seeds; 95% bootstrap CI over 78 subjects). Non-temporal effect (encoder and training regime): EncoderNet minus SleepCNN; temporal-layer effect: ContextSleepNet minus EncoderNet (differences of per-subject ∆MF1). ∗/∗∗: Holm-corrected Wilcoxon p < 0.05/0.01 over the eight W4A4 contrasts. FP8 first/last rows are shown for reference; they lie outside this family and carry no stars.

Table 10: Single-layer sensitivity: ∆MF1 (pp, 95% CI) when only the named layer is quantized to W4A4 and all others stay FP32. Stars: Holm-corrected Wilcoxon p < 0.05/0.01 within the probes of each model (8 for SleepCNN, 18 for ContextSleepNet).

Table 11: Only the first layer quantized (all other layers FP32): weights only, input activations only, or both. ∆MF1 in pp (95% CI). ∗/∗∗: Holm-corrected Wilcoxon p < 0.05/0.01 over the twelve W-only and A-only conditions.
Table 12: Per-stage F1 (%), pooled over the 78 test subjects, mean over three seeds.
